This paper proposes RACE for improving the execution speed of robot manipulation policies. The initial reviewer scores were 6, 6, 2, and 8. Overall, reviewers agree that the paper is clearly written (despite some minor typos) and demonstrates strong performance in both sim and real environments.

The main concerns raised by multiple reviewers included:
 (1) missing ablation studies for the proposed TOPP and TTS components (zmC2, gaD1), and  (2) limitations of the method on quasi-static tasks (gaD1, XTQT).

In the rebuttal, the authors provided the requested ablation results as well as additional experiments on semi-dynamic tasks, which adequately address the shared concerns.

The remaining rejecting reviewer XTQT (score: 2) primarily questioned the novelty and impact of the work, arguing that it mainly integrates established control engineering techniques into VLAs.

From the AC’s perspective, accelerating imitation learning based policies is an important and timely problem. Integrating approaches from optimal control is valuable for the community and constitutes a novel contribution of this work. 

Based on the overall reviewer feedback and the authors’ rebuttal, the AC recommends accepting the paper. The authors should carefully proofread the manuscript and incorporate all promised revisions in the final version.

To further address Q5 and test RACE with external object dynamics, we additionally conducted experiments on semi-dynamic task. The robot has to pick moving juice pack on conveyor belt and put into a basket. Speed of the robot is crucial in this task as it leads to task failure when the robot is slow and miss the moving object. 

**Experiment Setup.** We collected 106 demonstrations and further fine-tuned $\pi_{0.5}$ fine-tuned on DROID dataset that was used in Section 4.2.2 to make the policy aware of external dynamic of the object. We tested with both original speed of conveyor belt and 2.5$\times$ speed of conveyor belt to see if RACE can generalize to unseen object speed. We used the base policy and base policy (15Hz) with 3$\times$ fast-forwarded actions (45Hz) as baseline for comparison.

| Method | SR | Time (s) | SOD | Fast SR | Fast Time (s) | Fast SOD |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Demonstration | 1.00 | 12.9 | 1.00 | — | — | — |
| Base (15Hz) | 0.03 | 21.3 | 0.61× | 0.00 | — | — |
| Base (45Hz) | 0.27 | 15.4 | 0.84× | 0.00 | — | — |
| **RACE (Ours)** | **0.63** | **9.8** | **1.32×** | **0.53** | **6.4** | **2.02×** |

(Fast: 2.5$\times$ Conveyor Belt Speed, SR: Success Rate, SOD: Speedup over Demonstration, Bold: best value)

**Results.** RACE achieves highest success rate and speedup for both original and 2.5$\times$ conveyor belt speed, demonstrating its efficacy for semi-dynamic, speed-demanding task. Furthermore, the performance degradation between original and 2.5$\times$ conveyor belt speed is minimal, achieving high generalization to external dynamic change, while other baselines fail completely. This shows that even without explicitly modeling external dynamic, RACE can work effectively when external dynamic can be take accounted by the IL policy except extreme cases like catching a ball. Videos for the experiment can be found in https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1rYCzep18xELz6ItSJvJXPf03xi9SUeG2?usp=drive_link.

Videos for the experiment can be found in https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1rYCzep18xELz6ItSJvJXPf03xi9SUeG2?usp=drive_link.

**Q1.** `How does RACE scale with the state space of the robot? if the robot is a humanoid, what are some of the considerations to adapt RACE to it?`

RACE scales efficiently to high-dimensional systems because the core planner (TOPP-RA) has linear computational complexity with respect to path discretization points, regardless of state dimension. While the cost of projecting dynamic constraints scales with state dimension, it remains computationally manageable for standard humanoid models. Consequently, it readily scales to bimanual manipulation, covering the upper-body control of a humanoid.

However, adapting to whole-body humanoid control introduces general challenges inherent to the domain, such as underactuation (floating base) and strict balance criteria (e.g., ZMP constraints). While these could theoretically be incorporated into our constraint formulation, we leave the specific adaptation to whole-body dynamics as a direction for future research.

**Q2.** `What is the effect of increasing the size of controllable state set? will this result in better time parameterizations?`

As explained in response to W1, TTS prevents TOPP failure from asynchronous misalignment by maximizing the volume of the initial controllable set, resulting in better time parameterization. We will make this relation between objective of TTS and TOPP clearer in the revision.

**Q3.** `What is the point of testing the methods with no inference delay?`

The experiment setting without inference delay is designed to **isolate the performance degradation caused by state error and reachability** from the errors caused by asynchronous misalignment. This **decouples the two fundamental challenges** RACE addresses. The results in Section 4.1.1 demonstrate that even without delay, naive acceleration fails due to physical constraints, validating the necessity of the "Desired State as Action" and "TOPP" components independent of the inference pipeline.

**Q4.** `Is there any point of using test-time search when there is no inference delay?`

Yes, though the benefit is less pronounced. Even without inference delay, TTS can contribute by smoothing the stitching between consecutive chunks and maximizing the controllable set size, which helps the planner find solutions for aggressive maneuvers. However, because planner failure is significantly exacerbated by the misalignment caused by inference delay, the primary impact of TTS is observed in the asynchronous setting.

**Q5.** `Does RACE work in non-quasistatic environments. For instance, playing air-hockey.`

As the reviewer has thankfully acknowledged on strengths of our work, `Speeding up policy execution while maintaining performance is an exciting area of research and has real-world impacts`. While RACE primarily works for quasistatic environments, its impact is still large, as the **vast majority of practical manipulation tasks are quasi-static**. Examples include industrial assembly, logistics (packaging), cooking, and domestic cleaning (as demonstrated in our experiments). In these domains, "speed" is the primary bottleneck for economic viability, while achieving high precision and generalizability is also crucial, highlighting the potential of our work. 

Finally, we claim that training reactive policies for extremely dynamic tasks, such as the mentioned air hockey, is a separate challenge. While RACE would ensure the robot moves as fast as physically possible to intercept a target, the policy itself would likely need to be trained specifically for such dynamic interception (predicting puck motion) rather than just accelerating a static demonstration. Our goal is to unlock the physical speed limits of the robot for the broad class of manipulation tasks where the robot—not the environment—is the limiting factor.
We thank the reviewer for their thoughtful review and for confirming that your concerns have been addressed.

I sincerely appreciate the time the authors have invested in their work and the care taken in responding to my comments. However, I am inclined to maintain my score for the following reasons:

1. As the authors have agreed, the contribution of this work is the **integration of existing control techniques into VLAs.** However, I observe little (if any) specialization to VLAs in particular and asked questions to verify this. An example of specialization would be considering the controllability of object manipulation, etc. However, it seems that the contributions are a natural side effect of viewing the “action chunks” of VLAs as trajectory proposals that must be re-optimized for a specific robot embodiment. “Action chunking” is a recent term that has overshadowed a history of work in real-time planning where compensating for computational, mechanical, and electrical time delays were not only common but absolutely necessary for effective autonomy (Kuwata et al., Findeisen and Allgöwer). Naturally, I wonder, if these control techniques were proposed to control a car to follow a racing line, would it be held in the same regard? Or, is the application to VLAs simply _that_ important?
2. Because control engineering under altered geometries has always been so effective, it would also be surprising to me if industry engineers would not already attempt these techniques even if they were not in a research paper. However, I acknowledge the value of contributions that demonstrate that an approach is indeed possible.
3. Reliance on rule-based, low-level controllers is generally adverse to more intelligent and safe policies. The inability of the robot to execute the trajectory at sufficient speeds is certainly not the fault of the robot but the imitation learning paradigm. In other words, VLAs themselves are drastically underutilizing their robotic embodiments largely due to abstracting away low-level planning and control. Obviously, this is not a contribution expected of the authors but an observation that “generalist policies” continue to heavily rely on low-level controllers which naturally bring about the necessity of post-processing modules such as the proposed work. I believe it may be dangerous to specialize low-level control thereby enabling VLA systems to continue to ignore this crutch.

Again, I reiterate my acknowledgement that industry engineers may benefit from learning about this work due to its more short-term solutions for VLA issues. However, I believe this is already sufficiently apparent via the feedback of other reviews. In offering a dissenting opinion, I wish to firmly maintain my current review.


**References**

Kuwata, Y., Teo, J., Fiore, G., Karaman, S., Frazzoli, E., & How, J. P. (2009). Real-time motion planning with applications to autonomous urban driving. IEEE Transactions on control systems technology, 17(5), 1105-1118.

Findeisen, R., & Allgöwer, F. (2004). Computational delay in nonlinear model predictive control. IFAC Proceedings Volumes, 37(1), 427-432.

**Q1-1.** `Given the extensive optimal control prior (model-based trajectory optimization), are iLQR or MPPI valid baselines? If so, why not compare them? `

We acknowledge that iLQR and MPPI also utilize robot dynamics. However, we did not use them as baselines because they solve a computationally different problem than the components of RACE (TOPP and TTS):
1. TOPP vs. General MPC: TOPP is a **specialized algorithm** for Time-Optimal Path Parameterization. It solves a 1D optimization problem to find the **exact minimum-time profile** along a **fixed geometric path**. In contrast, iLQR and MPPI are general trajectory optimizers that typically require fixed time horizons or complex hand-crafted cost functions to approximate time-optimality [1, 2]. They are computationally heavier and do not inherently guarantee the global time-optimality for a specific path that TOPP provides.   
2. TTS vs. General MPC: While TTS fits the broad description of MPC, replacing it with off-the-shelf iLQR/MPPI would lose the specific benefits detailed in W2. Specifically, standard MPC methods rely on gradient or random sampling (risking unnatural motions), whereas our TTS uses the imitation policy as a sampler to preserve human intent. Furthermore, standard MPC objectives (e.g., effort, tracking) do not explicitly target the asynchronous misalignment problem, which we solve via our novel smoothness-based controllability objective.

**Q1-2.** `I surmise by “explicit alignment to physical properties remains less explored”, the authors mean that physical constraints are not often included in MPC and CEM. This is certainly not true considering that MPC has traditionally been performed with models and actuation constraints and is actually often the baseline for model-based control. Here is an open-source project for manipulation with joint-level control under constraints: (Bhardwaj et al.).`

Our statement regarding "explicit alignment to physical properties remains less explored" refers specifically to the **learning-based control literature** (e.g., Model-Based RL, Imitation Learning), rather than the broader field of classical Optimal Control. In this specific learning context, optimization often relies on learned value functions rather than rigorous physical constraints. We fully agree with the reviewer that physical constraints are foundational to classical MPC and Control Theory. As detailed in our response to W2, our contribution is precisely bridging this gap: we introduce the rigorous constraint handling of classical optimal control into the inference loop of imitation policies to solve physical constraint violation and asynchronous misalignment. We will clarify this distinction in the revision.

[1] Williams, Grady, Andrew Aldrich, and Evangelos A. Theodorou. "Model predictive path integral control: From theory to parallel computation." Journal of Guidance, Control, and Dynamics 40.2 (2017): 344-357.
[2] Sundaralingam, Balakumar, et al. "Curobo: Parallelized collision-free robot motion generation." 2023 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA). IEEE, 2023.

I believe that the three main contributions are primarily established control engineering techniques. The slow execution rate of demonstration data necessary for learning reflects a fundamental limitation of the imitation learning paradigm, which is ideally not addressed by downstream control engineering. If we consider the domains in which these techniques are applicable, it is necessarily quasi-static problems where the dynamics of the task are wholly controllable by the agent. This would exclude eventual dynamic tasks like playing ping pong, throwing and catching, or anything else involving external dynamics not rigidly attached to the robot. In this sense, there is relatively shallow vision aside from the integration of these techniques into VLA systems.

However, control engineering has always yielded reliable sub-systems for autonomous systems and, naturally, current industry engineers relying on VLA systems stand to benefit from learning about this work. Beyond this, it is challenging for me to envision how other researchers may fundamentally build upon what is presented.

weaknesses.value:
On contributions
1. “Imitation from states instead of actions” is effectively learning-from-observation but this area’s related work is not discussed at all. For instance, learning an inverse dynamics model might be a valid and more generalizable alternative to this works’ model-based trajectory optimization.

    * In the first place, if the “action” is not the robot actuation (e.g. motor commands) but some function of state, the learning problem did not originally have actions to begin with. This is an important distinction because almost all robot actions are underactuated relative to state. Hence, this is why modern VLAs rely heavily on controllers to do position control, but the modern language and this work seems to have equivocated delta state as actions. In other words, the first claimed contribution of “actions as state” implicitly existed already in standard VLAs.

    * In the way it is presented, I must assume that the model used for the Time-optimal planning pertains only to the robot (it would be a significantly different and substantial contribution to apply time-optimal planning for exteroceptively sensed states, like a manipulated hammer or ball). This also implies that following controllability and reachability analyses are done only on robot state. However, under this scope, these analyses effectively reduce to optimal control for trajectory tracking. Reachability is often otherwise used in safety analyses for domains such as autonomous driving or social navigation where unsafe and dynamic constraints can be highly non-convex and correlated across uncontrollable states (Bansal et al.).

2. Test-time search and controllability. As noted in the related works, this is very much equivalent to MPC.

3. The work acknowledges that many of the individual techniques exist with a substantially rich history in the related works. I appreciate that the authors do not overclaim the contributions. However, it is perhaps misleading to dedicate such large portions of the manuscript (sections 3.1-3.3) to existing techniques. The authors may save on space by citing references and discussing integration or system-wide challenges rather than the individual methods. For instance, section 3.2 uses state as the time-optimal model parameterization, but states in the context of VLAs and their pertinent tasks are much more than just the robot state.

4. Parts of the paper are not well-proofread and remain unpolished:
   * Caption of figure 7

We sincerely appreciate the reviewers' insightful feedback and positive evaluation. Most reviewers agreed that **(1) the problem setting has real-world impact**, addressing the speed bottleneck in practical manipulation tasks (Reviewer gaD1, XTQT), **(2) simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate superior performance of RACE** (Reviewer zmC2, gaD1, XTQT, qRQC), and **(3) the presentation is clear** (Reviewer zmC2, gaD1, XTQT). During the rebuttal, we addressed the reviewers' concerns, leading Reviewer gaD1 to explicitly increase the score (**6 --> 8**). Below, we organize how we addressed initial concerns, and further clarify on the remaining concerns.


### Summary of Addressed Concerns

Here, we organize our actions regarding the primary concerns on broader applicability (**Non-quasistatic Tasks & External Dynamics**), clarification of contribution (**TTS Role, Novelty & Ablations**, **System-Wide Challenges**, **Design Choice Clarity**) and presentation of related works and background (**Background on TOPP**, **Related Work & Comparison**). (TTS: Test-time Search, TOPP: Time Optimal Path Parameterization)

| Concern | Response |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Non-quasistatic Tasks & External Dynamics** (gaD1 Q5; XTQT W0 & W1-3) | **We conducted experiments on a semi-dynamic task.** We tested RACE on a "moving object on conveyor belt" task. Results demonstrate minimal performance degradation even as the object speed increases to 2.5x (unseen during training), proving RACE handles predictable external dynamics effectively. |
| **TTS Role, Novelty & Ablations** (zmC2 W1; gaD1 W1-3 & Q2 & Q4; XTQT W2) | **We clarified the interdependency of TTS and TOPP and conducted ablations.** We explained that TTS enables TOPP by maximizing the initial controllable set ($\mathcal{K}_0$) and distinguished it from general MPC. We also added component-wise ablations proving TTS drives success/consistency while TOPP drives speed. |
| **System-Wide Challenges** (XTQT W3-2) | **We added a "System-Wide Challenges" discussion.** We expanded the manuscript to detail practical integration challenges to highlight novelty, including queue management with timestamps for stochastic delays and constraint margins for robustness. |
| **Design Choice Clarity** (gaD1 W4) | **We added illustrative examples.** To further motivate design choices, we added concrete examples contrasting State vs. Action (tracking geometry), TOPP vs. Naive (handling sharp corners), and TTS vs. Naive Async (correcting drift). |
| **Background on TOPP** (zmC2 W2; XTQT W3-1) | **We balanced rigor with conciseness.** We added formal notation for dynamics and projection (addressing zmC2) while condensing the general background text (addressing XTQT) to focus on the novel integration aspects. |
| **Related Work & Comparison** (XTQT W1-1 & W1-2 & Q1) | **We expanded the Related Work section.** We incorporated "Learning-from-Observation" and explicitly clarified the differences and superiority of RACE compared to general MPC approaches in the context of accelerated imitation. |


### Clarification Regarding Reviewer XTQT's Remaining Concerns

We first note that Reviewer XTQT also acknowledged our **clear motivation, presentation, effectiveness of RACE for accelerating IL policies and its usefulness in practical settings**, such as industrial tasks. However, the reviewer questions the significance of the contribution, characterizing it as a "short-term solution" integrating "existing control techniques" that allows IL systems to "ignore the crutch" of low-level control. We respectfully argue that this is a misunderstanding of our work and clarify the contributions as follows:

(1) **Novel Components**: Beyond the TOPP solver, RACE’s core components—Test-Time Search (TTS) with controllability objectives and Desired State as Action—are novel contributions designed specifically for generative policies, not off-the-shelf control techniques.

(2) **Novel Integration**: Grounding probabilistic, generative action chunks with deterministic optimal control like TOPP is a non-trivial, under-explored problem fundamentally different from static trajectory tracking.

(3) **IL-Specific Challenges**: This integration solves unique challenges—stochastic latency and generative bifurcation—that cause TOPP solver to fail, which we solve by using TTS to maximize controllability.

(4) **Physical Awareness**: RACE does not allow policies to "ignore" physics; it enforces Test-Time Physical Alignment, using TTS to steer the policy into physical feasibility.

(5) **Foundational Bridge**: Combined, RACE provides a principled, policy- and embodiment-agnostic bridge between high-level semantic reasoning and low-level physical actuation, rather than a short-term patch.

**W3-1.** `The work acknowledges that many of the individual techniques exist with a substantially rich history in the related works. I appreciate that the authors do not overclaim the contributions. However, it is perhaps misleading to dedicate such large portions of the manuscript (sections 3.1-3.3) to existing techniques.`

We appreciate the constructive feedback on the manuscript's structure. While integration of TOPP into the generative action chunking pipeline is our novel contribution, the detailed exposition of TOPP (Section 3.2) was intended to establish the necessary mathematical notation required to derive our novel smoothness-based controllability objective in Section 3.3 and the proofs in Appendix B. However, we agree that the description of standard TOPP-RA can be condensed. We will shorten the general background in Section 3.2 by referencing the original paper (Pham & Pham, 2018) more heavily and moving the details to Appendix.

As the reviewer validly pointed out, the core contribution lies in the integration into a generative action chunking pipeline. We clarify that Sections 3.1 (State-based Targets, detailed in W1-2) and 3.3 (Smoothness Objective, detailed in W2) represent novel design choices enabling this integration. We will use the space saved from condensing the background to elaborate on this core contribution, how each components contribute, and system-wide challenges during integration (detailed in response to W3-2).

**W3-2.** `The authors may save on space by citing references and discussing integration or system-wide challenges rather than the individual methods. For instance, section 3.2 uses state as the time-optimal model parameterization, but states in the context of VLAs and their pertinent tasks are much more than just the robot state.`

We deeply appreciate the suggestion to discuss system-wide challenges. In addition to existing discussion on asynchronous inference and discarding actions (Line 212-225), we will add the following discussion in the revision:
1. **Interdependency of TTS and TOPP**: As noted in the manuscript (Line 205-206), a time-optimal solution does not always exist if the initial state is not controllable (i.e., outside $\mathcal{K}_0$). We will explicitly clarify that TTS serves as a key enabler for TOPP in the integrated system: by maximizing the volume of the initial controllable set (as evidenced by Figure 7b), TTS effectively reduces the frequency of planner failures caused by asynchronous misalignment. 
2. Queue Management with Action Timestamp: Since action chunks are generated and consumed asynchronously across the imitation policy, path planner, and low-level controller, we attach precise execution timestamps to each action based on its inference start time. This ensures correct temporal ordering under inference delays and avoids executing outdated action chunks.
3. Margin for Kinodynamic Constraints: In real-world hardwares, kinodynamic constraint violation lead to abrupt stop of the robot. To avoid this, we apply slightly tightened constraint values during path planning, providing a small robustness margin while still enabling high-speed execution.

**W4.** `Parts of the paper are not well-proofread and remain unpolished (e.g., Caption of figure 7)`

We apologize for the caption error in Figure 7 and will correct it, together with other typos and minor issues pointed out by other reviewers in the revision.

We thank the reviewer for their helpful comments and for acknowledging the strength of our paper. We appreciate the opportunity to clarify RACE's operation regarding action chunks and constraints.

**W1.** `RACE requires the backbone policy to output the entire state trajectory. It can't accelerate policies that only produce single actions or action sequences.`

We clarify that RACE operates with policies that generate **local action chunks** (sequences of fixed horizon, e.g., $T_a=16$), **not** the entire global state trajectory of the task.

As detailed in Section 3.2, RACE applies Time-Optimal Path Parameterization (TOPP-RA) locally to the "state trajectory generated by the action chunk policy". Specifically, RACE interpolates the generated action chunk—which is a sequence of state waypoints—using a cubic spline to define a local path $q(s)$ for that specific window. This process is repeated in a receding horizon fashion, seamlessly connecting these chunks.

Consequently, RACE is fully compatible with modern imitation learning models that output action sequences (chunks). In our experiments, we demonstrated this compatibility by applying RACE to Diffusion Policy (which predicts chunks of $T_a=16$) and the VLA model $\pi_0$ (which predicts chunks of $T_a=8$ or $15$).

**W2.** `When using TOPP-RA, RACE needs accurate knowledge of the robot’s physics constraints, such as maximum torque and velocity.`

We view the reliance on physical constraints as a practical strength rather than a limitation. Standard kinematic and dynamic limits are **widely available for commercial robots** (e.g., in URDFs), and users can simply define conservative constraints to ensure safe operation if exact limits are unknown. Our real-world experiments demonstrate that using standard model constraints allows RACE to achieve 4x acceleration on high-precision tasks without violating hardware limits.

**Q1.** `Does RACE's performance drop down when the backbone policy does not output the entire trajectory?`

We clarify that performance **does not drop**, as RACE is explicitly **built for chunk-based policies**. All reported results were achieved using policies that predict short-horizon chunks (e.g., $T_a=8$ or $16$).

**Q2.** `Several typos in the paper need correction: citation errors in line 46, 82, 85, "chang,e" in line 361, missing a space in line 320.`

We thank the reviewer for the careful reading and apologize for the oversights. We will thoroughly proofread the manuscript to correct all typos and ensure citation accuracy in the final revision.

We thank the reviewer for acknowledging the practical utility of RACE for industry applications. However, we respectfully disagree with the characterization that our work is merely a "short-term solution" that allows IL systems to "ignore the crutch" of low-level control, or that it is a trivial application of existing control techniques and real-time planning methods (e.g., Kuwata et al., Findeisen & Allgöwer).

We believe this view stems from a misunderstanding of how RACE integrates with the IL paradigm. We address this by clarifying five key points. (1)-(3) address the first and second concern regarding novelty and contribution of our work. (4) addresses third concern regarding letting the policy ignore low-level control. (5) addresses the viewpoint that states our work as short-term solution for IL/VLA issues:

(1) **RACE components are novel adaptations, not just existing control techniques.** While we utilize Time-Optimal Path Parameterization (TOPP) as a solver, the surrounding components are novel contributions designed for the generative nature of IL policies.

- Test-Time Search (TTS) is not standard MPC: Standard MPC/real-time planning typically optimizes for tracking error or control effort. Our TTS optimizes for controllability volume and smoothness to specifically counter the stochastic misalignment caused by inference delays and improve TOPP success rate.
- Desired State as Action: This is a novel re-formulation of the imitation target to enable acceleration, distinct from standard inverse dynamics or tracking control.

(2) **The integration of TOPP into Generative AI is a novel conceptual contribution.** This integration using optimal control to ground generative AI is a non-trivial and under-explored scientific problem. For instance, the reviewer asks if applying control to "follow a racing line" would be held in the same regard. This is fundamentally different because a "racing line" is a static, geometrically consistent path derived from a known model. In contrast, action chunk from generative policies is a probabilistic sample from a generative model that is often inconsistent with prior chunks or the current robot state due to inference latency. RACE does not just "track" a path; it mediates between a probabilistic semantic planner and a deterministic physical system, ensuring that generated behaviors are translated into physically valid execution.   

(3) **Solving IL-specific challenges beyond historical delay compensation.** Indeed, using optimal control to ground these generative policies poses non-trivial challenges that go beyond historical delay compensation and real-time planning (e.g., Kuwata et al., Findeisen & Allgöwer). These methods typically address computational delays in deterministic optimization loops where latency is bounded and the planner is consistent. RACE addresses a different class of problems specific to generative policies:

- Large, Stochastic Latency: IL/VLA inference times are highly variable and significant (e.g., 0.1s or more) compared to real-time control loops.   
- Bifurcation & Inconsistency: Unlike a geometric planner, generative policy may output chunks that are topologically inconsistent with the previous chunk due to state drift during latency. 

Crucially, these large latencies and action inconsistencies often render the robot's state uncontrollable with respect to the new plan, causing the Time-Optimal Path Parameterization (TOPP) solver to fail. RACE solves this via Test-Time Search (TTS), which explicitly selects action chunks that maximize the volume of the controllable set, ensuring that a valid time-optimal solution exists even under severe asynchronous misalignment. 

(4) **RACE makes policies aware of low-level control, not ignorant of it.** The reviewer expresses concern that RACE allows the policies to "continue to ignore this crutch" of low-level control. We argue the exact opposite: RACE acts as a Test-Time Physical Alignment mechanism. By utilizing the policy as a sampler and the physics-based planner as a scorer (via TTS), we are explicitly injecting physical awareness into the policy's execution loop. This mechanism effectively bridges the gap between data-driven, probabilistic semantic planning and deterministic physical execution, steering the policy into physical feasibility rather than allowing it to violate low-level constraints.

(5) **A pioneering bridge, not a short-term patch.** Ideally, foundational models would internalize all robot dynamics. However, retraining massive VLAs for every specific robot embodiment's dynamics is often computationally intractable. RACE provides a principled, policy- and embodiment-agnostic bridge (requiring only a standard model like a URDF). It allows generalist semantic agents to function safely and efficiently on specific physical hardware. We believe this constitutes a concrete step towards bridging the gap between high-level reasoning and low-level actuation in robotic foundation models.

We deeply appreciate the thoughtful review and suggestions for improvement.

The main concern from the reviewer is the contribution of our work. We believe it would be beneficial to clarify a few aspects of the **problem setting** (**accelerating imitation policies** vs. control engineering), hence the novelty and contribution of our integration.

Our main contribution is **improving Imitation Learning (IL) system** by borrowing concepts from optimal control, in which the **integration of optimal control itself is a novel contribution** that is less explored in the IL literature, *not* improving the optimal control method itself. More specifically, our method accelerates the execution speed of imitation policies while maintaining their precision and generalizability, achieving **best-of-both-worlds**: versatility of IL and speed of optimal control. 

Below, we address each concern one by one to clarify our contribution and explain why this is a non-trivial problem, even with concepts from optimal control literature. 

(From Summary) `If we consider the domains in which these techniques are applicable, it is necessarily quasi-static problems where the dynamics of the task are wholly controllable by the agent. This would exclude eventual dynamic tasks like playing ping pong, throwing and catching, or anything else involving external dynamics not rigidly attached to the robot. In this sense, there is relatively shallow vision aside from the integration of these techniques into VLA systems.`

First, thank you for recognizing the potential of our method. As the reviewer has commented, `current industry engineers relying on VLA systems stand to benefit from learning about this work`. While this is already a large domain which robots are used for, applicability of our work goes beyond this, as the vast majority of practical manipulation tasks are quasi-static. Examples include industrial assembly, logistics (packaging), cooking, and domestic cleaning (as demonstrated in our experiments). In these domains, "speed" is the primary bottleneck for economic viability, while achieving high precision and generalizability is also crucial. This highlights the **importance of the problem** given that IL, VLA systems can achieve high precision and generalizability while speed becomes key bottleneck to their practical applications. The ability to execute a precise insertion or a packaging task 2-4x faster than human demonstration (as RACE achieves) directly translates to doubled or quadrupled throughput. 

Finally, we claim that training reactive policies for extremely dynamic tasks, such as the mentioned throwing and catching, is a separate challenge. While RACE would ensure the robot moves as fast as physically possible to intercept a target, the policy itself would likely need to be trained specifically for such dynamic interception (predicting object motion) rather than just accelerating a static demonstration. Our goal is to unlock the physical speed limits of the robot for the broad class of manipulation tasks where the robot—not the environment—is the limiting factor.

**W1-1.** `“Imitation from states instead of actions” is effectively learning-from-observation but this area’s related work is not discussed at all. For instance, learning an inverse dynamics model might be a valid and more generalizable alternative to this works’ model-based trajectory optimization.`

Thank you for pointing out the related work. We will add learning-from-observation as related work in the updated manuscript.

Unlike prior works in learning-from-observation, we directly train the model to output robot states (pose or configuration). Compared to prior works in learning-from-observation, such as the inverse dynamics model the reviewer mentioned, **our approach offers distinct benefits in our problem setting (accelerating imitation policies)**:
1. Our method **can adaptively adjust the acceleration rate** to satisfy kinodynamic limits, while prior learning-from-observation cannot, and has to use a fixed acceleration rate. In this case, an action that leads to the desired state may simply not exist due to the constraints, hence the inverse dynamic approach may fail.
2. Our method **doesn't require additional data**, while prior learning-from-observation methods need additional accelerated trajectory data to transfer from the original (inverse) dynamic to the accelerated (inverse) dynamic.
Thank you for your thoughtful review and for confirming that your concerns have been addressed.

summary.value:
The authors propose an approach to speed up policy inference at inference time. Their proposed method, RACE, uses states as imitation actions, optimizes for the timing of state chunks, and employs a sampling-based replanning mechanism for asynchronous execution. Experiments are conducted in both sim and real, testing the task success rate v.s. speedup rate. Ablations are done to showcase lower state deviation and higher smoothness of the method.

Overall, the motivation of the paper is clear, the method is sound, and the experiments results are strong. However, I have a few questions/concerns that could be addressed by the authors to further improve the paper. I'm happy to raise my score if the concerns are properly addressed.

comment.value:
**W1-2.** `In the first place, if the “action” is not the robot actuation (e.g. motor commands) but some function of state, the learning problem did not originally have actions to begin with. This is an important distinction because almost all robot actions are underactuated relative to state. Hence, this is why modern VLAs rely heavily on controllers to do position control, but the modern language and this work seems to have equivocated delta state as actions. In other words, the first claimed contribution of “actions as state” implicitly existed already in standard VLAs.`

We clarify that "action" in the paper refers to input of the robot controller during teleoperation (which can be a function of state), as the standard convention in IL, where "state" refers to the actual **reached state** during teleoperation, which is **different from the input state given by the action**. For instance, if action is an absolute state or delta state, inputs to the controller (e.g., PD controller or OSC controller) are states. However, due to underactuation (i.e., controller error), the actual reached state of the robot differs from the input state. This distinction becomes critical when accelerating the policy as controller error increases. 

Path of "reached states" in the demonstration are **geometric (dynamic-invariant)**, hence can be used as imitation target regardless of acceleration rate. This distinction and employement of **reached state as imitation target** in our method differs from standard approaches in IL or VLAs.

**W1-3.** `In the way it is presented, I must assume that the model used for the Time-optimal planning pertains only to the robot (it would be a significantly different and substantial contribution to apply time-optimal planning for exteroceptively sensed states, like a manipulated hammer or ball). This also implies that following controllability and reachability analyses are done only on robot state. However, under this scope, these analyses effectively reduce to optimal control for trajectory tracking. Reachability is often otherwise used in safety analyses for domains such as autonomous driving or social navigation where unsafe and dynamic constraints can be highly non-convex and correlated across uncontrollable states (Bansal et al.).`

Reachability discussed in the paper is exactly in the context of actuation feasibility for trajectory tracking, rather than collision safety, since **scope of our work is acceleration**. The core problem of acceleration is torque saturation. If we speed up a trajectory by 4x, the required acceleration scales by 16x. Without a model, the robot will violate torque limits and deviate from the path. RACE uses time-optimal planning with the robot's dynamic model to analytically determine the maximum valid speed along the generated geometric path. This ensures the robot executes the task at the limit of its physical capability, but never beyond it. We leave expanding this to external object dynamics or safety constraint to future work.

**W2.** `Test-time search and controllability. As noted in the related works, this is very much equivalent to MPC.`

We view both Test-Time Search and MPC as broad conceptual frameworks for horizon-based optimization. Consequently, the novelty of our approach lies not in the general framework itself, but in the specific design choices that instantiate it for accelerated imitation—choices that distinguish it from prior MPC literature:
1. Imitation Policy as Sampler: Instead of the random noise or gradient-based sampling common in standard MPC, we utilize the imitation policy itself as a generative sampler. This design choice constrains the search to the manifold of human-like behaviors, ensuring the accelerated trajectory remains natural rather than just physically feasible.
2. Novel Objectives for Asynchronous Inference (Smoothness & Controllability): While standard MPC typically minimizes tracking error or control effort, we introduce smoothness and controllability volume as test-time objectives. These are not standard performance costs; they are designed to maximize the robustness of the handover between asynchronous chunks. By explicitly selecting trajectories that maximize the volume of the feasible state-space (via smoothness), we address the specific problem of misalignment caused by inference delays—a challenge in accelerated asynchronous policies that standard MPC objectives do not target.

**W1.** `The test-time search part of the algorithm seems to be disconnected from the rest, and the objective to optimize for smoothness seems a little arbitrary. Is this component added just to overcome some issues of asynchronous inference, or does it have some ties with the time-optimal planning (Section 3.2)?`

Thank you for asking to clarify the motivation for Test-time Search (TTS) and connection to time-optimal path parameterization (TOPP). While misalignment of action and state due to asynchronous inference is key motivation for adoption of TTS, the **design of TTS directly ties to TOPP**. 

As noted in the manuscript (Line 205-206), a time-optimal solution does not always exist if the initial state is not controllable (i.e., outside $\mathcal{K}_0$). TTS serves as a key enabler for TOPP in the integrated system: by minimizing curvature (maximizing smoothness), TTS reduces the required acceleration to follow the path. This effectively **maximizes the volume of the initial controllable set**, as evidenced by the "Controllability" metric in Figure 7b. By increasing the size of $\mathcal{K}_0$, TTS **reduces the frequency of planner failures** caused by asynchronous misalignment. We will explicitly clarify this relationship between the TTS objective and TOPP feasibility in the revision.


**W2.** `The authors should also try to explain whether the test-time search component can prevent issues from (Black et al. 2025, Figure 2), where bifurcation between consecutive chunks can exist.`

Thank you for raising this excellent point. Our TTS method indeed **prevents issues like bifurcation** (where the policy abruptly changes between two modes, such as going left vs. right), which is quantitatively supported by the **increased "Consistency"** metric in Figure 7b.

We first recall that Consistency is defined as the negative Euclidean distance between the new action chunk and the executed segment of the previous chunk at the handoff point (Appendix D.5). A **bifurcation event manifests as a low Consistency metric**, as the policy switches between distinct modes (e.g., from a 'left' trajectory to a 'right' one), creating a large spatial discontinuity at this handoff point. As shown in Figure 7b (bottom left), RACE achieves **higher Consistency scores by incorporating TTS**. By selecting chunks that minimize curvature given the current robot velocity (boundary condition), TTS naturally **penalizes candidates that sharply diverge from the current trajectory**, thereby suppressing bifurcation and smoothing transitions between asynchronous updates. We will add this discussion on bifurcation scenarios and emphasize the ablation result in the revision.

**W3.** `Following the previous point, there seem to be ablations missing: what is the performance when you remove time-optimal planning and only include test-time search, and vice versa?`

Thank you for suggesting ablation study that can further help clarify the contribution of TTS. We've conducted additional ablation studies by excluding each components (TOPP, TTS), using Square and Tool Hang, the most precision-demanding tasks in Robomimic:

|               |   Square   |            | \|  | Tool Hang  |            |
|:------------- |:----------:|:----------:|:--- |:----------:|:----------:|
| **Method**    |   **SR**   |  **SOD**   | \|  |   **SR**   |  **SOD**   |
| **RACE (Ours)**      | ***0.86*** | ***1.74*** | \|  | ***0.62*** | ***1.86*** |
| w/o TTS       |    0.81    | ***1.74*** | \|  |    0.59    |  **1.85**  |
| w/o TOPP      |  **0.85**  |    1.42    | \|  |  **0.61**  |    1.36    |
| w/o TOPP, TTS |    0.82    |    1.43    | \|  |    0.59    |    1.39    |

(SR: Success Rate, SOD: Speedup over Demonstration, Bold & Italic: best value, Bold: second best value)

Result shows that **TOPP leads to higher speed**, while **TTS leads to higher success rate**. Consequently, RACE with both components achieves the Pareto-optimal result. This demonstrates that both TOPP and TTS are key components for achieving high speedups (nearly 2x demonstration speed) while maintaining high success rates.

Additionally, our real-world ablation results in Figure 7b show that Throughput (a combined metric of speed and success) increases by more than 1.5$\times$ with the addition of TTS. This demonstrates that TTS is even more critical for performance on real hardware where physical constraints are strictly enforced.

**W4.** `The method section describes multiple design choices and their reasoning (using state vs. actions, using a high-gain PD controller vs. time-optimal planning, naive asynchronous execution vs. test-time search), but they can be improved with examples. It will be beneficial to include visual explanations in addition to the text.`

Thank you for the suggestion. We will incorporate the following concrete examples into the revision to clarify these design choices:
1. State vs. Action: During teleoperation, a user might provide a gentle "move forward" command. If executed 4x faster, a standard controller might overshoot due to momentum. RACE treats the reached state (position) as the target and uses a stiff, high-gain controller to track that geometry precisely, rather than just replaying the motor commands.
2. TOPP vs. Naive Acceleration: Consider a pick-and-place motion where the robot transitions from a vertical lift to a horizontal transfer. This creates a sharp corner in the path. A naive 4x speedup would demand torque exceeding motor limits at this turn, triggering a protective stop. TOPP anticipates this bottleneck, automatically slowing down just for the high-curvature segment to satisfy torque constraints, then aggressively accelerating on the straight transfer sections.
3. TTS vs. Naive Async: Due to inference delay, the robot might be drifting slightly left while the new plan assumes it is centered. Naively executing the new plan would cause a "jerk" to the right. TTS samples multiple future chunks and selects one that curves smoothly from the current leftward velocity, preventing control instability.

**W5.** `There are apparent typos, incomplete captions, and citation errors throughout the paper. Here are some examples. The authors should fix these and spend effort double-checking the paper for errors.`

We thank the reviewer for the careful reading and apologize for the oversights. We will thoroughly proofread the manuscript to correct all typos, complete the captions, and ensure citation accuracy in the final revision.

summary.value: The paper proposes RACE, a method that accelerates robot policies beyond expert demonstration speed. RACE uses TOPP-RA to refine the state trajectories proposed by the learned policy, generating new trajectories that satisfy physical constraints. When inference delays occur as in real-world settings, it applies Best-of-N sampling over action chunks to maximize trajectory smoothness. Experiments on Lift, Can, Square, and Tool Hang tasks show that RACE outperforms baselines in both simulation and real-world environments.

strengths.value:
1. The paper conducts extensive experiments across four manipulation tasks in both simulation and real-world environments. To evaluate RACE’s robustness and trajectory quality at test-time, the paper designs rich metrics including action smoothness, joint error, and consistency.
2. Real-world demos are provided, showing that RACE performs well at different control rates (15Hz, 30Hz, 45Hz).
3. RACE can accelerate various backbone policies learned by imitation with no additional training in the backbone policy, like diffusion policy and VLA.

1. RACE requires the backbone policy to output the entire state trajectory. It can't accelerate policies that only produce single actions or action sequences.
2. When using TOPP-RA, RACE needs accurate knowledge of the robot’s physics constraints, such as maximum torque and velocity.

1. Robot Configuration ($q$): We will define $q \in \mathbb{R}^n$ as the robot's joint configuration vector (angles) and $\mathcal{C}(q)$ as the feasible torque polytope.
2. Dynamics Terms: We will explicitly identify the terms in the dynamics equation $A(q)\ddot{q} + \dot{q}^\top B(q) \dot{q} + f(q) \in \mathcal{C}(q)$, where $A$ is the mass matrix, $B$ contains Coriolis/centrifugal terms, and $f$ represents gravity/friction.
3. Dynamics Projection: We will clarify that the standard TOPP-RA projection substitutes the chain rule relationship $\ddot{q} = q'(s)\ddot{s} + q''(s)\dot{s}^2$ into the dynamics equation. This transforms the high-dimensional constraints into linear scalar constraints on the path state $x=\dot{s}^2$ and control $u=\ddot{s}$.

**Q1.** `Is it possible to establish a Pareto front by, for example, changing the constraints in TOPP?`

While it is theoretically possible to trace a Pareto front by artificially lowering the velocity and torque limits (e.g., to 50% or 80%), doing so provides no practical benefit in our setting. As shown in our experiments (Figures 4 and 5), RACE already achieves success rate of the original policy. Since the success rate is already maximized (bounded by the original policy's capability), lowering the limits would only reduce execution speed without yielding any gain in accuracy. Therefore, our result represents the optimal operating point under physical limits—maximizing speed while maintaining peak success rates—rather than just one point on a trade-off curve.
